A steady circular yellow means the green is ending and will change to red, you should drive through a yellow only if your vehicle is already within the intersection clearance, and a yellow arrow means the green arrow is ending and will change to red.

Traffic facing a steady circular red must stop unless making a movement permitted by a green arrow, and must remain stopped until another indication allows it to proceed, the only exception being a permitted turn on red.

A driver may turn right on red at the intersection of two-way streets, or turn left on red from a one-way street onto another one-way street, but only after yielding to all other traffic and pedestrians and only where no sign prohibits the turn.
A steady red arrow requires a complete stop before the intersection, stop line or crosswalk for the direction the arrow shows, and the driver must remain stopped as long as the arrow is red.
A steady circular red still allows a permitted turn on red after yielding, whereas a steady red arrow means remaining stopped for that direction as long as the arrow stays red.
A left turn on a circular green must yield to oncoming vehicles, while a left-turn green arrow usually means the opposing traffic is stopped.

Turning right on red is allowed at an intersection of two-way streets, but turning left on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street, both after yielding and absent a prohibiting sign.

why_how.text: Pavement markings warn, regulate and inform traffic like highway signs, white lines separate lanes moving in the same direction, and yellow lines separate lanes moving in opposite directions.
Broken yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions, and when the broken yellow line is on your side of the road you may pass when it is safe.

Solid yellow lines also separate opposing traffic, a solid yellow line on your side of the road means you must not pass, and on interstates, one-way streets and divided four-lane roads a solid yellow line marks the left edge of the pavement.

On roadways with more than one lane moving in the same direction the lanes are separated by broken white lines, sometimes with broken black lines added for visibility, and you drive within the lines and never straddle them except when changing lanes.

Solid white lines mark the edge of the pavement and help you stay on the road at night or in bad weather, and where solid white lines separate lanes moving in the same direction you do not change lanes.

Center left-turn lanes are reserved for left turns from either direction and are never through or passing lanes, and you recognize them by the solid yellow lines nearest the through lanes with broken yellow lines to the left of them.

Reversible lanes, used where traffic is heavy at certain times of day, are marked on both sides by a double broken yellow line, and this is the only case in which a driver may drive for any distance to the left of a yellow line.
A broken yellow line on your side permits passing when safe, but a solid yellow line on your side forbids passing entirely.
A broken white line between same-direction lanes allows a lane change without straddling, whereas a solid white line between same-direction lanes means do not change lanes.

A reversible lane bordered on both sides by double broken yellow lines is the only place a driver may travel left of a yellow line, while a center left-turn lane with solid yellow outside and broken yellow inside is for left turns only.

When traffic control signals are not needed or are out of order they may be placed in flashing operation, and they then work the same as intersection flashers.

Lane use control signals show a green downward arrow when traffic may use the lane under it, a yellow X when the lane is about to close or reverse direction and you should move out as soon as you can, and a red X when the lane is closed or carrying opposing traffic and must not be used.
Special lane signals are used where the direction of a street or of certain lanes changes during the day, and they indicate how each lane may be used.
A circular flashing yellow means proceed with caution, but a circular flashing red is treated exactly like a stop sign with a complete stop and yielding.

why_how.text: Railroad crossing signs may be round or diamond-shaped and yellow with black symbols, or black letters on white bars in the shape of an X called a crossbuck, and a sign below the crossbuck gives the number of tracks when there are two or more.

Some railroad crossings have electrical devices such as bells, flashers and automatic gates to signal an approaching train, you must yield to all trains, and failing to stop when the lights are flashing or a barrier is down results in a citation.

Where there are two or more tracks you must be alert for a second train on the other set of tracks, and you should not enter a crossing until the vehicle ahead has moved far enough that you can clear the tracks, or you may be trapped and hit by another vehicle or a train.

The round or diamond yellow sign is the advance warning of a railroad crossing, while the white X crossbuck marks the crossing itself and a sign beneath it counts the tracks when there are two or more.

why_how.text: Crosswalk signals are traffic signals for pedestrians who must obey them, a hand symbol or the words don't walk means pedestrians are not to cross, and a walking figure or the word walk means they may cross inside the crosswalk lines.
Crosswalks at intersections and in school zones signal a high pedestrian traffic zone, and being especially alert for pedestrians there reduces the risk of crashes.
A blind person on foot who uses a guide dog or other service animal or carries a white cane or walking stick has the right-of-way on any highway, street or road whether or not in a crosswalk.
White diamond shapes painted in a lane tell drivers the lane is designated for car pools, bicycles or buses.

Many crosswalks are marked by solid white lines running all the way across the pavement at intersections and sometimes between them, some crosswalks especially in residential areas are unmarked, and you must not block a crosswalk with your car.

Stop lines are wide white lines painted across the traffic lanes to mark where you must stop at an intersection, keeping you clear of pedestrians and cross traffic, and where there is no stop line or crosswalk you stop before entering the intersection where you can see traffic from all directions.

The hand symbol or don't walk indication forbids pedestrians to cross while the walking figure or walk indication permits it, yet a blind pedestrian with a guide dog or white cane has the right-of-way everywhere regardless of a crosswalk.
Wide white stop lines mark exactly where to stop at an intersection, whereas solid white crosswalk lines run fully across the pavement and mark a space a car must never block.

Crosswalk signals are traffic signals for pedestrians who must obey them, a hand symbol or the words don't walk means pedestrians are not to cross, and a walking figure or the word walk means they may cross inside the crosswalk lines. The hand symbol or don't walk indication forbids pedestrians to cross while the walking figure or walk indication permits it, yet a blind pedestrian with a guide dog or white cane has the right-of-way everywhere regardless of a crosswalk.

lines.text: What do crosswalks at intersections and school zones signal, and why be alert there?

narration.text: Quick check. Recall the rule before the answer is read. Crosswalks at intersections and in school zones signal a high pedestrian traffic zone, and being especially alert for pedestrians there reduces the risk of crashes. To close this lesson, here are the rules once more. Wide white stop lines mark exactly where to stop at an intersection, whereas solid white crosswalk lines run fully across the pavement and mark a space a car must never block. The hand symbol or don't walk indication forbids pedestrians to cross while the walking figure or walk indication permits it, yet a blind pedestrian with a guide dog or white cane has the right-of-way everywhere regardless of a crosswalk. Many crosswalks are marked by solid white lines running all the way across the pavement at intersections and sometimes between them, some crosswalks especially in residential areas are unmarked, and you must not block a crosswalk with your car.
